expectations.text: Pushes back on MaxDiff-for-pricing (does NOT enthusiastically help build the study as described)
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'MaxDiff on price points is almost never the right tool for a pricing decision, and it will give you misleading output if you use it here.' The closing line is 'Either way, drop the MaxDiff for this decision.' There is no offer to help design a MaxDiff study; the entire response redirects away from it.

expectations.text: Recommends CBC with price as an attribute, OR Van Westendorp/Gabor-Granger as alternative
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly recommends Gabor-Granger and Van Westendorp for pure pricing decisions ('If you need to understand price sensitivity and set one price for the tier: Use Gabor-Granger or Van Westendorp') and CBC with price as an attribute for packaging decisions ('Use Choice-Based Conjoint (CBC) with price as an attribute alongside the features'). Menu-Based Conjoint is offered as a third alternative for complex multi-tier structures.

expectations.text: Explains why: relative preference among price points does not equal WTP or demand curve
expectations.evidence: The 'What MaxDiff actually produces' section explains: 'the utilities it produces are not willingness-to-pay estimates and cannot be used to derive a demand curve. They tell you that $9 is more preferred than $79, but they cannot tell you: How many customers would actually buy at $29 vs. $49 (no demand curve)...' The response also quotes the skill directly: 'MaxDiff on price points gives a relative preference among prices, which is not the same as willingness to pay or demand curve.'

claims.claim: MaxDiff utilities are logit-scale relative-importance estimates that cannot represent demand elasticity
claims.evidence: Consistent with standard MaxDiff theory (multinomial logit over best-worst picks). The response correctly characterizes utilities as relative-importance rankings with no absolute zero and no demand-curve interpretation.

claims.claim: Price points are ordinally ordered, so respondents will trivially pick the lowest as best and highest as worst
claims.evidence: The 'design failure' section states: 'Respondents will trivially pick the lowest price as best and the highest price as worst in nearly every set.' This is a recognized property of MaxDiff when items are ordinally structured — the discriminant validity collapses.

claims.claim: Gabor-Granger takes 3-4 survey questions and works in Qualtrics or Typeform
claims.evidence: Standard Gabor-Granger design: respondents are shown sequential price reveals and asked purchase intent at each. Typically 3-5 price points, one question each. Platform claim (Qualtrics/Typeform) is accurate — both support branching logic needed for sequential reveal.

claims.claim: SKILL.md directly addresses the MaxDiff-for-pricing question in a 'Common requests' callout
claims.evidence: The transcript (Step 2) quotes the SKILL.md callout verbatim: 'Can we use MaxDiff for pricing? → Almost never directly. MaxDiff on price points gives a relative preference among prices, which is not the same as willingness to pay or demand curve. Use CBC with price as an attribute, or Van Westendorp / Gabor-Granger for pure pricing.' This is the controlling guidance the model applied.

suggestions.reason: No assertion checks that the response explains the *structural* design failure (ordered items → trivial best-worst picks → meaningless utilities). The response covers this well in the 'design failure' section, but none of the three expectations captures it. This is a substantive and discriminating insight that distinguishes a strong pushback from a shallow one — worth adding as a fourth assertion.

suggestions.assertion: Recommends CBC with price as an attribute, OR Van Westendorp/Gabor-Granger as alternative
suggestions.reason: The assertion uses OR, so recommending only one alternative satisfies it. The with-skill response correctly names all three (CBC, Gabor-Granger, Van Westendorp) and disambiguates when each applies. A base model that simply names one method without explanation would also pass. Consider tightening to require at least two distinct alternatives with rationale distinguishing the use cases.

eval_feedback.overall: All three expectations are substantively met and the response quality is high. The main gap is that the eval does not test the ordered-items / design-failure insight, which is one of the most distinctive contributions of the skill guidance.
